overview: This map’s “Bengal” outline from 1783 to 1800 is not an independent Bengali kingdom. The English East India Company had held the Mughal grant to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa since 1765, while nawabi authority was steadily reduced. The polygon stretches beyond the Bengal delta and then vanishes at the atlas’s 1800 seam; Company government, farming, weaving and family life continued.

periods.title: Company government before the permanent land settlement
periods.summary: Revenue experiments and new courts placed growing power in Company hands, while older offices and local intermediaries remained important.

periods.title: Permanent Settlement and the Cornwallis Code
periods.summary: The 1793 system fixed the Company’s land-revenue demand on zamindars and reorganized courts and district administration.

sections.title: Who ruled, and who collected the rent?

items.text: The Company’s 1765 diwani grant concerned revenue collection in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. By the 1780s this commercial corporation was also acting like a territorial government. Calling the region simply “Bengal” hides both the Mughal legal frame and the Company’s expanding coercive power.

The Cornwallis reforms created detailed rules for revenue, courts and district officers. Indian advisers still helped colonial judges interpret Hindu and Muslim law, but senior authority was concentrated in European officials. A district map cannot show the chain of clerks, interpreters, petitioners and local power holders who made government function.

The Permanent Settlement of 1793 fixed the amount owed by zamindars to the Company and treated estates as saleable property. If revenue was not paid on time, estates could be auctioned. One policy could therefore change a landlord’s fortune while leaving cultivators to face demands from several layers of rent collectors.

Most people lived in the countryside and depended on agriculture. Zamindars stood above a large cultivating population, but “peasant” did not mean one identical household. Land rights, tenancy, occupation, religion, gender and local ecology all shaped who had security and who carried the risk of a bad harvest.

Bengal’s cotton and muslin production depended on skilled household labor. A 1798 or 1799 Solvyns print shows a weaver at a simple loom; its accompanying account also notices children contributing to family earnings. The image is an outsider’s selective observation, not permission to treat child labor as quaint.

Company purchasing and overseas demand tied weaving villages to distant consumers. Over time, colonial policy and British industrial competition weakened Bengal’s export position and pushed many artisans toward cultivation or other work. That change was uneven; a famous muslin did not protect every spinner or weaver from debt and pressure.

A 1799 etching of a Calcutta bazaar preserves stalls, baskets, customers and sellers in an open market. It cannot tell us the price of dinner, but it restores ordinary exchange to a history often crowded by governors. Food and household goods moved through many such small transactions.

Money itself required expertise. Sarrafs tested and exchanged coins, arranged bills of exchange and helped zamindars make revenue payments in the required sicca rupees. Their networks linked treasuries, mints and commercial houses. Think of a currency counter, credit office and emergency revenue fixer sharing one desk.

Rivers were roads. Solvyns’s 1799 “pansway” shows a small passage boat used for inland travel around Calcutta. Boats carried people and goods through a landscape where seasonal water could make an overland route inconvenient or impossible. A ferry schedule was useful technology even when nobody printed it.

sections.title: Learning, medicine and the bathroom question

items.text: The Calcutta Madrasa began in 1780 and passed to Bengal government support in 1782. Its teachers trained a limited group in Persian, Arabic and Muslim law for work in courts and offices. This was specialized education for male students, not universal schooling and not evidence that girls or village children had equal access.

The Asiatic Society was founded in Calcutta in 1784 and soon gathered manuscripts and published research. Its early membership was European-only, so its achievements came with a sharp social boundary. The manuscripts and knowledge it collected often depended on Indian scholars, scribes and older intellectual traditions.

A General Native Hospital for Indian patients opened in Calcutta in 1792. Earlier Company hospitals largely served soldiers and employees, and one 1789 letter even argued about admitting officers’ servants. A hospital building therefore existed, but it did not mean most families had easy, trusted or free medical care.

The checked sources do not support a claim that late eighteenth-century Calcutta had universal sewers, piped household water or standardized toilets. Markets, tanks, courtyards and drains all affected health, but later sanitary reports cannot safely be projected backward as a precise 1790s bathroom plan. The honest toilet fact is that the paperwork arrived more clearly than the plumbing.

Charles Wilkins developed Bangla metal type at Hooghly, and the Bengali craftsman Panchanan Karmakar learned and helped make the letters. Halhed’s 1778 grammar became the first book printed with this new Bangla type. The technical achievement belonged to punch cutting, casting, composing and press work as much as to the English author named on the title page.

A tiny writing sample from the 1778 printed alphabet is অ আ ই ঈ, modernly transliterated a, ā, i, ī. These are Bangla vowel letters. The Unicode line here transcribes the old printed forms rather than pretending to reproduce their exact ink shapes, and modern pronunciation does not map perfectly onto one English vowel each.

Printing made repeated letterforms possible, but it did not instantly replace manuscripts. The Asiatic Society’s earliest gifts in 1784 included Persian manuscripts, while Bengali, Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian writing continued in many settings. A press joined a busy manuscript world instead of switching it off overnight.

ending.text: Nothing special happened to Bengal in the atlas year 1800. Company rule and the Permanent Settlement continued, Calcutta remained a political and commercial center, and the Company’s territorial state expanded. Crown rule replaced Company government only in 1858. The map’s disappearing polygon is therefore a data seam, not the fall of Bengal or the end of Bengali society.
